reference.view_jobs: A relationship needs a structured view when the reader must follow how parts relate, not only what each is. The kinds, each with the view that carries it: hierarchy or belonging (a tree); a call path from an entry to its effect (a call path); ordered steps with evidence (a trace); ordered work with branches (a flowchart or flow); participants exchanging messages over time (a sequence diagram); states and transitions (a state diagram); boundaries, ownership and dependencies (a board with arrows); records, identity and cardinality (an entity diagram); numeric change across ordered categories (a chart); the same facts compared across several items, when the section sets them out for the reader to compare (a table); alternatives on corresponding topics (a comparison); exact source, schema, configuration or commands the reader must inspect (a code view); a few headline numbers, each with its meaning and a comparison (stats); one named component, option or finding with its depth (a card). A simple fact or an interpretation needs no separate view: prose under a purposeful heading carries it. An opening summary that previews what the page goes on to explain leads with the answer and needs no view of its own; the sections that explain those points are judged on their own. A list or run of points that each stand alone, such as scope items, open questions, status, constraints or quotations, is not a relationship, even when it is long.

examples.text: Prose: 'A request enters the gateway, which checks the token with the auth service, then forwards it to the orders service, which writes to its own database and emits an event the billing worker consumes.' Views: none.
examples.needs_view: yes: a path through several parts

examples.text: Prose: the same request path. Views: a sequence diagram of gateway, auth service, orders service and billing worker.
examples.views_carry: yes: the diagram shows the path the prose explains

examples.text: Prose: 'The release was cut on Tuesday. It includes the faster search and two bug fixes; nothing in it changes stored data.' Views: none.
examples.needs_view: no: simple facts and an interpretation

examples.text: Prose: explains how an order moves from created to paid, shipped or cancelled, and which events cause each move. Views: a table of the team's on-call rota.
examples.views_carry: no: the table shows another subject

examples.text: Prose: compares three storage options on cost, latency and durability. Views: a table with one row per option and those three columns.
examples.needs_view: yes: the same questions for several items
examples.views_carry: yes: the table carries the comparison

examples.text: Prose: a first paragraph explains how a request passes through the gateway, the auth service and the orders service; three paragraphs follow about the release checklist and who signs it off; then a sequence diagram of the request path ends the section.
examples.needs_view: yes: a path through several parts
examples.views_carry: no: the diagram shows the path, but it sits after unrelated points, not next to the paragraph it supports

examples.text: Heading 'Open questions'. Prose: four bullets, each naming one undecided item and who decides it.
examples.needs_view: no: points that each stand alone, not a relationship

examples.text: Prose: explains how a payment moves from authorised to captured or refunded, and in passing names the team that owns the payment service. Views: a state diagram of the payment's states, right after that explanation.
examples.views_carry: yes: the payment's states, explained in detail, have their view next to the explanation; the owning team is only named in passing and needs none

examples.text: A table of four release decisions; one cell explains, step by step, how a failed deploy rolls back through three services. No view shows that rollback.
examples.needs_view: yes: a path explained in detail inside one cell
examples.views_carry: no: the rollback is explained in detail and no view shows it, even though the table carries the decisions

reference.next_to: Next to means a reader finds the view where they read about its point: right before or after the passage that explains it, or after a short run of paragraphs on that same point. A run of points that one view draws together counts as one passage. A view is away from its text when it sits past unrelated points or other views, or so far from its passage, such as at the end of a long section, that the reader has to hunt for it.

reference.detail: Long detail sits one action away (a tab, a disclosure, a linked page) so nothing becomes a text wall. Optional depth is what a reader can skip and still follow the page's open questions and conclusions: history and earlier decisions, rationale, evidence, receipts, provenance such as exact quotes behind a summary, inventories, reference data, and trace or index tables that map items to their owners, interfaces or proofs, even when one column names failures. That holds even when the table is the whole of its section. Content the reader needs in view stays: the exact corresponding facts a comparison or choice on the page rests on, a contract or core mapping the page is about, and a table whose subject is failure cases with their thresholds. A disclosure holds only the rationale or evidence about failure cases, never the cases themselves. Content carried from a source keeps its form and initial state; that can't be seen on the page.

instructions.task: Is table optional depth that a reader can skip and still follow the page's open questions and conclusions, rather than content the reader needs in view?

criteria.true: The table, as it reads with its heading and lead-in, holds background or supporting depth as reference.detail defines it: history, rationale, evidence, receipts, provenance, inventories, reference data, or a trace or index that maps items to owners, interfaces or proofs, even when one of its columns lists failures, which a trace cross-references rather than sets out.
criteria.false: The table, as it reads with its heading and lead-in, holds what the reader must compare or check: the exact corresponding facts a comparison or choice rests on, a contract or core mapping, or failure cases and their thresholds as the table's own subject.

instructions.task: Is table long enough that reading or scanning it in the main path holds up the section's point, the way a wall of text would?

criteria.true: Taking the table in costs real reading relative to its point, so a reader who skips it saves real time: enough entries, dense cells, or both, whatever the cells hold.
criteria.false: The table is short or compact: a few rows, or a small matrix of ids or short entries a reader takes in at a glance.

instructions.task: Does table set out failure cases or their thresholds as its content, rather than rationale or an option's gains and costs that mention a failure in passing?

criteria.true: Rows or cells of the table state cases where something fails or is refused, or the limits at which it does.
criteria.false: The table names no failure case or threshold, or mentions one only in passing within rationale or an option's gains and costs.

yes.finding: This table sits in a closed disclosure and states failure cases or their thresholds; check whether they belong in view, then decide.
